The house style for figures: one theme with its colors, shapes and line types, readable labels, and one way to save a figure at its printed size.

::: {.Rcode title="Source code"}
The full R script is available at:

-   [`R/plot_style.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/COHERO-RCT-analysis/blob/main/R/plot_style.R)

This R script file is itself reliant on the following helper files:

-   [`R/setup.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/COHERO-RCT-analysis/blob/main/R/setup.R)

The code sections below are imported directly from that script when this page is rendered.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
#| cache: false
knitr::read_chunk("../R/plot_style.R")
```

## Check the ggplot2 version

The theme relies on features added in ggplot2 4.0.0: a theme can carry the palettes its figures use, and labels can be looked up by variable name. On an older version the script stops with a message saying what to update, rather than failing later with a less helpful error.

```{r}
#| label: check-ggplot2-version
#| eval: false
```

## Palettes

A palette is the ordered set of colors (or shapes, or line types) given to the groups in a figure. The colors are the Okabe-Ito set, chosen to stay distinguishable for people with the common kinds of color-vision deficiency, with a neutral dark gray first so the control arm recedes and the intervention arm stands out. Groups also differ by point shape and line type, so a figure still works in grayscale and never relies on color alone.

```{r}
#| label: publication-palettes
#| eval: false
```

## The publication theme

A theme controls everything in a figure that is not data: background, gridlines, text sizes, legend position. `theme_publication()` keeps only what helps a reader: light horizontal gridlines to read values against, thin axis lines, no panel border. It also carries the palettes above, so a figure needs no color settings of its own. Text sizes are set for the printed figure (9 points by default), so a figure should be saved at the size it will be printed.

```{r}
#| label: theme-publication
#| eval: false
```

## Labels

`label_figure()` replaces column names with readable names, and arm codes with arm names; this project passes `figure_labels` and `arm_labels` (defined on [Setup](setup.qmd#figure-labels)), giving "ACT score" rather than `act_score` and "Control" and "Intervention" rather than 0 and 1. `figure_label()` looks up one name, for titles and axis labels built in code. Both take the labels as arguments, so this file reads nothing from the rest of the project and can be copied with [`R/functions.R`](functions.qmd) into another one.

```{r}
#| label: label-figure
#| eval: false
```

## Saving a figure

`save_figure()` writes a figure at its printed size in millimetres, in each format needed: PDF and SVG, which keep lines and text sharp at any zoom, for journals; and PNG for the website. The PDF device embeds fonts and handles symbols such as the dagger (†). Nothing in the analysis saves a figure yet; this is the function to use when it does.

```{r}
#| label: save-figure
#| eval: false
```

## The default theme

Loading this file changes no settings. [Figures](figures.qmd#the-default-theme) sets `theme_publication()` as the default theme for this project, so another project that copies the file keeps its own default.

For more on themes and on choosing colors, see [Fundamentals of Data Visualization](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/) by Claus Wilke.
